The test image shows a corn ear with grayish-green to olive-green mold/fungal growth on kernels. This is an ear/seed disease.

Top candidates from the seed/pod part index: Aspergillus_Ear_Rot, Trichoderma_Ear_Rot, Fusarium_Disease, Diplodia_Ear_Rot, Gibberella_Disease.

Let me view reference images one at a time, exploring across classes first.
Trichoderma shows dark blue-green/black patches on kernels. The test image has a lighter, more powdery grayish-green mold. Let me check Aspergillus.
Very strong match. The Aspergillus reference shows olive-green powdery mold covering kernels, very similar to the test image. Let me check other candidates to be thorough.
Fusarium shows whitish-pink mold, not matching the green powdery mold in the test image. Let me check Gibberella.
Gibberella shows reddish/brown mold at the tip, not matching. Let me check Diplodia_Ear_Rot.
Diplodia shows grayish-brown mummified kernels, not the green powdery mold seen in the test image. Let me check Head_Smut and Common_Smut.
Head_Smut shows dark spore masses replacing the ear, not matching. Let me check Common_Smut on seed.
Common_Smut shows galls, completely different. Let me view a second Aspergillus reference to confirm the match.

This confirms the match. Both Aspergillus references show the same olive-green powdery mold on kernels that matches the test image. The test image displays:
- Olive-green to grayish-green powdery mold covering portions of the kernels
- Mold spread across the ear surface
- Kernels visible underneath with discoloration
- Characteristic dusty/powdery texture of Aspergillus

All other ear rot candidates (Trichoderma: dark blue-green patches; Fusarium: whitish-pink; Gibberella: red/pink; Diplodia: white mycelium/grayish-brown; Common_Smut: galls; Head_Smut: spore masses) are visually distinct from the test image.
